sections.content: A relatively entry-level to the intermediate course on comparative politics & regimes. While the actual content isn't as intimidating as the course name suggests, some still require quite a bit of study (i.e. Game Theory, different electoral systems). If you do study hard, you'll be home with a much more academic and thorough understanding of the world of politics.
sections.teaching:
Excellent professor. She always makes sure that your answers are answered, and tries to make the supposedly tedious topic into an interesting one. There are real-life examples and her lectures are a pleasure to take. She's got a funny accent btw which makes things even more 'entertaining'.

Best part about this course is you can choose pretty much any topics for your final essay (of course it has to be related to the course, say you can't discuss why Biden fell on his way to the plane, probably), and you can have a consultation session with Prof Hong before starting it.
sections.grading: Quite good on my part. Two exams and one essay, and that's pretty much it. I was slightly below mean in both exams, but still got within B range. Attendance is always checked.
sections.workload: Almost none. Just revision for exams and write the final essay.

sections.content: The course content itself is pretty interesting and easy to understand once you catch on. However, there are a lot of things to memorize (i.e.: different systems of voting and whatnot).
sections.teaching: The professor is nice, passionate, and willing to teach, but I found her powerpoint slides to be quite disorganized and difficult to follow. You really can't understand anything from just looking at the slides; she has to be there to explain it in person. For that reason, I didn't enjoy the class as much as I could have. The teacher does random checks of attendance, and is quite strict with it, so you do have to be aware of that.
sections.grading: This professor was especially kind when it came to grading, especially for this semester when there were many changes made to our academic year. Although it takes her a long time to grade, she was very generous with the final result. I didn't score very well in the midterm or the final, but still ended up with an A-.
sections.workload: I personally found the workload to be pretty manageable. There's not too much to be done so long as you keep up with the course content class by class, though it does pile up when you get to the midterm and final periods (there is a lot of content to memorize). The group project wasn't too stressful at all.

sections.content: The contents are quite comprehensive and I love the fact that I have a much better understanding of this topic after the course. But I think the content is a bit too easy for 3000 level. The only numerical part is game theory. If you study game theory before, it should be really really easy for you.
sections.teaching: Prof Hong is funny and nice and her teaching is wonderful. She explains the concepts clearly with an aid of abundant previous researches. She also cares about students' learning experience. I was not very into politics in the past. But after SOSC 3520, I feel like taking more politics related courses now. Unless you detest politics, you will like SOSC 3520.
sections.grading: Grading is good. You will get good grade if you work hard on essay and pay attention in class. I did not read the essential readings and still got A at the end. So the key is understanding the lecture notes thoroughly and paying more effort on essay writing. Consultation session for essay writing conducted by prof was very helpful which could help you finalize your essay direction.
sections.workload: Midterm, final, presentation and a 2000-word essay. Revision wise, workload is not heavy since the content is quite easy. As a business school student, presentation is not difficult in my opinion. I believe most people would find essay harder. So start early.

sections.content: Mainly the content comes from the textbook and there are around 12-14 topics throughout the semester. These topics contain a lot of basics in political science such as basic game theory in political science, democratic system, democratization, voting system, political censorship, resource curse etc.
sections.teaching: Prof. Jean HONG has great teaching skills. She's good at generalizing the content and explain the most interesting/important part to us and it's really helpful to understand the political world and political science. She's serious in teaching and appears demanding, but she's actually really nice and kind to answer questions and solve our problems.
sections.grading:
My grade is fairly good. We are assessed by presentation, mid-term, final exam, final paper and also random attendance checking.
The topic of presentations is determined by the professor and she will allocate the groupmates for you. But she will ask for your preferences on topics in the first class.
Mid-term and final share similar pattern, non-cumulative, focus on the readings and lecture notes, one week for preparation is enough but of course it's better you can read the assigned reading week by week.
Paper is the most demanding, 2500 words, topic can be determined by ourselves. Consultation session is provided. You need to spend effort in order to impress the instructor.
All in all, as long as you pay enough effort in this course, the grading will reflect your hard work.
